title: Tocar vs Jugar: Two Ways to Say “Play” in Spanish

meta_description: Tocar vs jugar: Spanish uses jugar for games and sports and tocar for instruments. Rules, regional jugar al vs jugar, other meanings of tocar and a quiz.
excerpt: Games and sports, or instruments? Spanish splits “play” in two.

body_html:
Tocar vs jugar is a pair that surprises English speakers, because English “play” covers games, sports, instruments and music. Spanish splits it: jugar is for games and sports, and tocar is for musical instruments. And tocar has several other everyday meanings, from “to touch” to “it’s your turn”. Here’s how to use both correctly, including the regional jugar al fútbol versus jugar fútbol.

Quick answer
  • Jugar = to play games and sports: jugar al tenis, jugar a las cartas.
  • Tocar = to play an instrument: tocar el piano.
  • To play music on a device: poner música.
  • Tocar also means to touch, to knock and “to be someone’s turn”: Te toca.
{{toc}}

Tocar vs jugar: the core rule

JugarTocar
Used forGames, sports, playing with toysMusical instruments
ExampleJuego al fútbol los sábados.Toco la guitarra desde niño.
Structurejugar a + game (in Spain and many countries)tocar + instrument (direct object)

Jugar: games and sports

  • jugar al fútbol / al baloncesto / al tenis to play football / basketball / tennis
  • jugar a las cartas / al ajedrez to play cards / chess
  • jugar a los videojuegos to play video games
  • Los niños juegan en el parque. The children are playing in the park.
  • jugar con + toy or person: jugar con muñecas, jugar con su hermano

The RAE dictionary records jugar a + game as the traditional construction, and also notes that the form without a is common in parts of the Americas.

Jugar al fútbol or jugar fútbol?

In Spain and much of the Spanish-speaking world, people say jugar al fútbol (a + el = al). In Mexico, Central America and other parts of Latin America, jugar fútbol without the preposition is very common. Both are understood; choose the one used by the people you talk to most.

{{image:2}}

Tocar: instruments and more

  • tocar el piano / la guitarra / la batería to play the piano / guitar / drums
  • ¿Tocas algún instrumento? Do you play any instruments?
  • La banda toca esta noche. The band is playing tonight.

Note the article: Spanish says tocar el piano, just like English “play the piano”.

Other meanings of tocar

  • To touch: No toques eso, quema. Don’t touch that, it’s hot.
  • To knock or ring: Tocan a la puerta. Someone’s knocking. / tocar el timbre to ring the bell.
  • To be someone’s turn: Te toca a ti. It’s your turn.
  • To win (a prize): Le tocó la lotería. She won the lottery.
  • To have to (fate or obligation): Hoy me toca trabajar. I have to work today.

Me toca works like me gusta: the thing that falls to you is the subject.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Playing music: poner, not tocar or jugar

To play a song on your phone or speaker, Spanish uses poner: Pon algo de música. (Put some music on.) / ¿Puedes poner esa canción otra vez? (Can you play that song again?). Saying jugar una canción is a direct calque from English and sounds wrong.

Conjugation note

Jugar has a unique stem change (u → ue): juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis, juegan. In the preterite, the first person adds a u: jugué. Tocar is regular, but the first-person preterite changes c to qu: toqué.

Real conversations

  • A: ¿Qué haces los fines de semana? (What do you do at weekends?)
  • B: Juego al pádel con mis amigos y toco la guitarra en un grupo. (I play padel with my friends and play guitar in a band.)
  • A: ¡Qué bien! ¿Cuándo tocan? (Great! When are you playing?)
  • B: El viernes. Te toca venir esta vez, ¿eh? (On Friday. It’s your turn to come this time, okay?)
{{image:3}}

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Juego el piano.Toco el piano.Instruments use tocar
Toco al fútbol.Juego al fútbol.Sports use jugar
Juega una canción.Pon una canción.Devices use poner
Es tu turno (in games, unnatural)Te toca.The natural phrase for turns
Jugé / tocéJugué / toquéSpelling changes in the preterite

Looking for more pairs where English uses one verb and Spanish two? Try {{link:pedir-vs-preguntar|pedir vs preguntar}} or browse {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

Try it yourself

Translate these sentences, then check your answers:

  1. My son plays the drums. (Mi hijo toca la batería.)
  2. Do you want to play cards? (¿Quieres jugar a las cartas?)
  3. Don’t touch the cake! (¡No toques la tarta!)
  4. Whose turn is it? (¿A quién le toca?)
  5. Play something by Shakira. (Pon algo de Shakira.)

If you got the last two right, you are already using tocar and poner the way native speakers do.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

In Spanish, you juegas games and sports, tocas instruments and pones music. Add te toca for “your turn” and you will sound natural at the park, at a concert and at the family games night.

faq.q: What is the difference between tocar and jugar?
faq.a: Jugar means to play games and sports. Tocar means to play a musical instrument, and also to touch, to knock or to be someone’s turn.

faq.q: Is it jugar al fútbol or jugar fútbol?
faq.a: Jugar al fútbol is standard in Spain and many countries. Jugar fútbol is very common in Mexico and parts of Latin America. Both are understood.

faq.q: How do you say “play a song” in Spanish?
faq.a: Use poner: Pon esa canción (Play that song). Jugar una canción is incorrect.

questions.explain: For playing music on a device, Spanish says poner.

questions.q: In a board game: Ahora te ___ a ti. (It’s your turn.)
Preterite, first person: Ayer ___ al ajedrez.
questions.explain: The g needs a u before e: jugué.
